cards.title: A household iron solved the mystery of credit card magnetic stripes
cards.body: In 1960, IBM engineer Forrest Parry struggled to combine magnetic tape with plastic security badges. Adhesives either warped the tape or ruined its magnetic properties. When he brought the problem home, his wife Dorothea suggested using a household clothes iron to melt the tape directly into the plastic base. Her quick experiment worked, creating the foundational technology used in billions of modern credit cards and identification badges today.

cards.title: The digital commands cut, copy, and paste were created to kill computer modes
cards.body: Before the 1970s, text editing on computers required switching between distinct modes for typing and deleting text. Computer scientist Larry Tesler sought to make editing intuitive. While working at Xerox PARC, he introduced the concepts of cut, copy, and paste. Inspired by traditional newspaper layout techniques of physically cutting paper with scissors and pasting it onto pasteboard, his commands transformed digital text editing forever.

cards.title: Hard drive heads fly above spinning disks at less than 10 nanometers
cards.body: Inside a hard disk drive, read-write heads float on a cushion of air generated by platters spinning at thousands of revolutions per minute. The distance between the head and the disk, known as the fly height, is under 10 nanometers. For scale, a single particle of smoke or a human hair is thousands of times thicker. Any microscopic dust particle striking the head causes a catastrophic disk crash.

cards.title: The invention of the blue LED took 30 years and won a Nobel Prize
cards.body: Red and green light-emitting diodes were invented in the 1960s, but creating a blue LED stumped scientists for three decades. Combining red, green, and blue light is essential to produce bright white light. In the early 1990s, scientists Shuji Nakamura, Isamu Akasaki, and Hiroshi Amano finally synthesized high-efficiency blue LEDs using gallium nitride. Their breakthrough enabled modern energy-saving white LED lighting, earning them the 2014 Nobel Prize in Physics.

cards.title: The standard "Hello, World!" program began in a 1970s Bell Labs memo
cards.body: Almost every novice programmer begins by writing code that outputs "Hello, World!" to the screen. This famous introductory convention was popularized by computer scientist Brian Kernighan. He first used the string in an internal 1974 Bell Labs memorandum about the B programming language. It gained global fame when he included it in the classic 1978 textbook The C Programming Language, cementing its place in software history.

cards.title: Weekend computer crashes inspired the invention of error-correcting code
cards.body: In the 1940s, mathematician Richard Hamming had to share computer time on Bell Labs punch-card mainframes. Over weekends, when operators were absent, machines frequently encountered error-prone read errors and aborted his calculations entirely. Frustrated by wasted compute time, Hamming argued that computers should not only detect errors but fix them automatically. In 1950, he published Hamming codes, enabling computers to silently correct digital data corruption without stopping.

cards.title: A single second is officially defined by over 9 billion atomic oscillations
cards.body: Before 1967, one second was defined as a fraction of Earth's rotational day. However, because Earth's rotation fluctuates slightly, scientists needed a perfectly constant reference. Today, the International System of Units defines one second as exactly 9,192,631,770 cycles of microwave radiation emitted during energy transitions in a caesium-133 atom. This extreme atomic precision forms the base timing for global telecommunications, navigation systems, and internet synchronization.

cards.title: A single 1968 presentation demonstrated the future of personal computing
cards.body: On December 9, 1968, computer scientist Douglas Engelbart delivered a 90-minute live presentation at the Fall Joint Computer Conference in San Francisco. Dubbed "The Mother of All Demos," Engelbart debuted experimental technology that defined modern computing: the computer mouse, interactive text editing, screen windowing, hypertext links, and real-time video conferencing. Remarkably, all these features operated seamlessly in a single working software system, decades before becoming mainstream.

cards.title: The network utility "ping" was named after submarine sonar pulses
cards.body: When network engineers want to check if a remote computer is reachable, they use the "ping" command. Computer scientist Mike Muuss wrote the tiny utility in 1983 to diagnose network connectivity issues. He named it after the sound pulses emitted by submarine sonar equipment, which echo back after striking distant underwater objects. Similarly, the ping command sends data packets across the network and measures how long they take to return.

cards.title: The word "algorithm" derives from a 9th-century Persian mathematician
cards.body: Long before digital computers existed, the foundational concept of step-by-step mathematical calculation was established. The modern word "algorithm" comes from the latinized surname of Persian astronomer and mathematician Muhammad ibn Musa al-Khwarizmi, who worked in Baghdad during the Islamic Golden Age. His 9th-century influential textbook introduced systematic algebraic methods to Europe, where his name al-Khwārizmī was eventually translated into the Latin term algorismus, evolving into "algorithm."

quizzes.question: What household item was used to successfully combine magnetic tape with plastic ID cards?
quizzes.explanation: Dorothea Parry used a household clothes iron to melt the magnetic tape directly into the plastic card without ruining the magnetic properties.

quizzes.question: Why did Larry Tesler invent the cut, copy, and paste commands at Xerox PARC?
options: To eliminate mode switches in computer text editing
To save hard drive storage space
To replace physical keyboards with mice
quizzes.explanation: Tesler wanted to eliminate complex mode switching, creating modeless editing inspired by physical paper layout techniques.

quizzes.question: Approximately how far above the spinning platter does a hard drive head fly?
quizzes.explanation: Hard drive read-write heads float on an air cushion less than 10 nanometers above the disk, far thinner than a human hair or smoke particle.

quizzes.question: Why was the breakthrough invention of the blue LED so critical for general lighting?
options: Blue LEDs use less heat than red LEDs
Combining red, green, and blue light produces white light
Blue light is easier on human eyes
Blue LEDs are made of cheaper silicon
quizzes.explanation: Combining red, green, and blue light produces white light, enabling energy-efficient LED bulbs for everyday use.

quizzes.question: Who popularized the famous standard introductory software string "Hello, World!"?
quizzes.explanation: Brian Kernighan popularized 'Hello, World!' in a 1974 Bell Labs memo and the 1978 book 'The C Programming Language'.

quizzes.question: What motivated Richard Hamming to develop error-correcting codes in 1950?
options: Unattended weekend mainframe crashes due to card reader errors
Errors in telegraph wire transmissions during WWII
quizzes.explanation: Hamming was frustrated that unmonitored weekend mainframe card errors wiped out his code runs, leading him to invent automatic error correction.

quizzes.question: Which atom's microwave radiation cycles officially define the length of a second?
quizzes.explanation: The International System of Units officially defines a second based on exactly 9,192,631,770 transitions of a caesium-133 atom.

quizzes.question: What landmark 1968 computer demonstration introduced the mouse, windowing, and hypertext?
quizzes.explanation: Douglas Engelbart's 1968 presentation was later dubbed 'The Mother of All Demos' for introducing foundational modern computing concepts.

quizzes.question: What real-world technology inspired the name of the network utility "ping"?
quizzes.explanation: Creator Mike Muuss named ping after the echo sound pulses of active submarine sonar.

quizzes.question: The word "algorithm" is derived from the latinized name of a mathematician from which historical era?
quizzes.explanation: It derives from the latinized name of Muhammad ibn Musa al-Khwarizmi, a 9th-century Persian scholar in Baghdad.

guesses.prompt: How high above a hard drive's spinning platter does the read-write head float, in nanometers?
guesses.explanation: Hard drive heads float on a thin cushion of air just under 10 nanometers above the spinning platter.

guesses.prompt: How many years passed between the invention of red/green LEDs and the invention of the blue LED?
guesses.explanation: Red and green LEDs arrived in the 1960s, but creating high-efficiency blue LEDs took three decades of research until the early 1990s.

guesses.prompt: How many atomic oscillations of caesium-133 officially define a single second?
guesses.explanation: A second is defined as exactly 9,192,631,770 microwave cycles of a caesium-133 atom.

misconceptions.claim: Credit card magnetic stripes were originally attached using industrial superglue.
misconceptions.explanation: Adhesives melted and ruined the magnetic tape; IBM engineer Forrest Parry's wife used a household clothes iron to melt the tape directly onto plastic.

misconceptions.claim: The digital concepts of cut, copy, and paste were modeled after physical newspaper layout techniques.
misconceptions.explanation: Larry Tesler adapted the terms and actions directly from traditional physical editing, where layout artists used scissors and pasteboards.

misconceptions.claim: The network command 'ping' was coined as an acronym standing for 'Packet InterNet Groper'.
misconceptions.explanation: Creator Mike Muuss stated that 'ping' was not an acronym; he named it after the sound pulses emitted by submarine sonar.

misconceptions.claim: The word 'algorithm' was coined in the 20th century by IBM computer scientists.
misconceptions.explanation: The word comes from 'algorismus', the Latin translation of the 9th-century Persian mathematician al-Khwarizmi's name.
